About this statement
This is Transpower’s first set of 
climate-related disclosures required 
by the Aotearoa New Zealand Climate 
Standards. It follows four years of 
previous voluntary climate-related 
disclosures, initially in Transpower’s 
integrated reports using the Task 
Force on Climate-Related Disclosures 
framework and most recently in 
a separate climate-related 
disclosures report.
1.	 To operate the grid, Transpower also owns and operates an extensive nationwide telecommunications network.
Transpower New Zealand Limited (Transpower) 
is the owner and operator of Aotearoa 
New Zealand’s electricity transmission network, 
the National Grid1. The grid is nationally significant 
infrastructure and a lifeline utility under the Civil 
Defence Emergency Management Act 2002. 
Transpower is a state-owned enterprise and 
a climate reporting entity under the climate 
change response Act (Zero Carbon) Amendment 
Act 2019.
Transpower’s climate statement has been 
prepared in compliance with the Aotearoa 
New Zealand Climate Standards (NZCS1, NZCS2 
and NZCS3) published by the External Reporting 
Board in December 2022.
Transpower has disclosed information where 
it is material as defined in NZCS3, namely that 
“information is material if omitting, misstating 
or obscuring it could reasonably be expected 
to influence decisions that primary users make 
on the basis of an entity’s climate-related 
disclosures”. 
Primary users of the climate statement are 
defined as Transpower’s current and future 
investors, lenders and other creditors, and 
insurance companies.
Transpower’s climate statement includes 
disclosures for Risk Reinsurance Limited (RRL), 
Transpower’s 'captive' insurance subsidiary.

Letter from the Chair
On behalf of the Board of Transpower, 
we are pleased to present the first 
Transpower Climate Statement, as 
required by the Aotearoa New Zealand 
Climate Standards.
Climate change is a significant driver for 
Transpower’s business, both as a risk to its 
infrastructure and performance and in the 
opportunity it presents as Aotearoa New Zealand 
seeks to decarbonise its economy through 
electrification. Transpower sits at the heart of 
this transition. 
Since 2020, the Board has overseen a systematic 
work programme aimed at articulating and 
reporting Transpower’s exposure to climate-
related physical and transition risks and its 
climate-related opportunities. 
In 2023 and in line with the Aotearoa New Zealand 
Climate Reporting Standard, Transpower 
developed temperature rise-based scenarios. 
These are consistent with the demand-based 
scenarios outlined in Whakamana i Te Mauri Hiko 
– Empowering our Energy Future, Transpower’s 
2020 publication that explores different energy 
demand and supply pathways. It provides further 
contextual clarity for how Transpower should 
govern, manage, measure and respond to the 
climate risks and opportunities it faces. 
This climate statement presents in detail the 
evidence-based approach taken to defining 
potential outcomes, identifying risks and 
opportunities, planning future activity and 
setting targets and key performance indicators. 
As well as fulfilling our statutory reporting 
requirements as a Climate Reporting Entity, 
this report reflects our Board’s commitment 
to support the electrification of our economy 
and mitigate the impact of climate-related 
events on the grid.
From here, we can continue our journey to 
a net-zero carbon economy, confident that 
Transpower is continuously evaluating the 
risks and opportunities presented by climate 
change and working towards a future of greater 
electrification as it continues to meet the needs 
of the communities it serves.

Overview
Aotearoa New Zealand has a target 
of net-zero emissions by 2050, which 
is driving the increasing electrification 
of its economy and communities. 
Transpower has a significant role to 
play in enabling the transition from 
a predominantly fossil-fuel based 
energy sector to one that is based 
on renewable resources.

3.	 Energy in New Zealand 2023 (mbie.govt.nz)
This country has a highly renewable electricity 
system by international standards (85 per 
cent for the 12 months ended 30 June 20242). 
However, when looking at energy consumption 
overall, fossil-fuel based sources still fulfil 
approximately 70 per cent of overall energy, 
mainly through transport and process heat3. 
This stark contrast underscores the challenge 
of transitioning from fossil fuel-based sources to 
renewable electricity to support the achievement 
of Aotearoa New Zealand’s net-zero targets. 
Transpower’s dual roles as owner-operator 
of the National Grid and operator of the 
electricity system place it at the centre of this 
transition. Transpower needs to enable the 
rapid connection of new renewable energy 
sources and increase the capacity of the grid to 
support these connections to meet increasing 
demand. At the same time Transpower must 
continue to operate a stable power system that 
seamlessly integrates more highly distributed 
and intermittent energy sources. 
Transpower expects electrification will gather 
momentum between 2025 and 2030 as changes 
in technology and cost make it feasible for 
businesses and households to meet more of their 
energy needs through electricity. Transpower 
will continue to progress initiatives to ensure it 
can integrate more electrification and renewable 
electricity into the grid at least cost while 
continuing to operate a stable power system.
Transpower must ensure its grid infrastructure 
and market system are fit for purpose to enable 
further electrification while meeting the risks 
and opportunities presented by climate change. 
These span both the physical risks to assets and 
the transitional risks that arise domestically as 
Transpower seeks to maintain a stable power 
system with increasing intermittent renewable 
generation. 
Rather than producing a separate climate change 
risk strategy, climate change is a core assumption 
underpinning Transpower’s business strategy and 
has been driving its strategic decision making 
for several years. The way Transpower identifies, 
manages, governs and responds to climate change 
risks and opportunities is embedded in its business 
operations and asset management approach.
Transpower’s strategy Transmission Tomorrow was 
refreshed in 2023, following the 2020 publication 
of Whakamana i Te Mauri Hiko. This report outlines 
Transpower’s strategic context. It identifies the 
different energy demand and supply pathways 
Aotearoa New Zealand could take in its transition 
journey through to 2050, and the implications of 
each for Transpower, the community in which it 
operates, and the electricity industry.
Whakamana i Te Mauri Hiko recognises climate 
change as a key pillar driving the global and 
national context which, in turn, drives Transpower’s 
strategy and operations.

In 2023 and in line with the Aotearoa New Zealand 
Climate Reporting Standard, Transpower developed 
temperature rise-based scenarios. These are 
consistent with Whakamana i Te Mauri Hiko 
and provide further contextual clarity for how 
Transpower should govern, manage, measure 
and respond to the climate risks and opportunities 
it faces. 
Numerous risks and opportunities arise from the 
electrification of the economy, bringing with them 
increasing demand and load, increasing customer 
connections and the need to strengthen the grid
and build additional infrastructure. These measures 
will result in increasing carbon emissions and 
the challenge for Transpower of maintaining 
its social licence to operate, building new grid 
infrastructure and influencing how regulatory 
frameworks can enable this. 
Transpower’s physical risks are associated with 
the increasing frequency and severity of extreme 
acute weather events, but also chronic hazards 
such as sea level rise. The risks are characterised 
by the impact that these events and hazards have 
on the operation of assets and the market system. 
Transpower’s assets are subject to a diverse range 
of natural hazards. Climate change is increasing
both the frequency and magnitude of many of the 
natural hazards that already occur. Transpower’s 
asset planning accounts for this changing dynamic 
by incorporating resilience to major hazards into 
its grid investments with awareness of climate 
change projections.

Transpower’s asset risk review process identifies 
and collects information for asset management 
purposes on all major hazards, including those 
related to climate change. This enables Transpower 
to make informed decisions about asset health and 
network risk, so it can maintain a safe and reliable 
network and realise improvements in resilience to 
natural hazards and climate change. 
Transpower anticipates supply chain and other 
procurement issues resulting from the global 
transition to electrification and the impact of 
climate change on manufacturing and supply 
chains—these cover both physical and 
transition risks.
In this climate statement, each of these areas are 
outlined in more detail, and provide supporting 
evidence for the position taken. 
Every part of Transpower’s value chain is covered 
in this statement4.

SECTION 1
Governance
The way in which climate risks and
opportunities drive strategic decisions
and are managed within Transpower’s 
operational footprint is fully integrated
into governance and management 
structures. 
1.1  The role of the Transpower Board
Transpower’s Board is the body responsible for 
governance of its strategic direction including 
oversight of climate-related risks and opportunities 
and their impact on the strategic direction.
The Board is currently made up of seven directors. 
As a state-owned enterprise, Transpower’s 
shareholding ministers, the Minister for State-
owned Enterprises and the Minister of Finance, 
appoint directors. The Board reviews Transpower’s 
strategic context annually, before refining and 
confirming Transpower’s strategy and business 
plan. Both the strategy and business plan are 
reflected in the FY2024 Statement of Corporate 
Intent, which is provided to shareholding ministers, 
and available on the website.
Transpower’s Statement of Corporate Intent 
includes its budget and key asset health and 
network risk service measures, performance 
against which is monitored by the Board monthly. 
The grid-related outcomes and targets relate to 
Transpower’s performance in delivering the work 
programme agreed with one of its regulators, 
the Commerce Commission, for its five-year 
regulatory control period.
Transpower also delivers an annual System 
Operator Service Strategic Plan to a second 
regulator, the Electricity Authority, with a five-
year outlook consistent with Transpower’s role 
as System Operator. This includes a focus on 
the operation of the power system as it evolves 
to meet the future of increasing electrification 
with increased renewable and intermittent 
generation, and the introduction of new 
technologies and distributed energy resources.
1.2  Board committees
Climate-related risks are reported to the Audit 
and Risk Committee quarterly via the risk 
management dashboard, and subsequently to 
the entire board. The Audit and Risk Committee 
also reviews risk appetite settings, climate 
scenarios and climate-related reporting before 
it recommends these for Board approval. 
The System Operator Committee governs 
Transpower in its role as System Operator, 
including consideration of the particular risks 
and challenges to operating the power system 
arising from climate-related risks such as winter 
peak challenges. It meets quarterly. 
Transpower provides an update on its sustainability
programme, which underpins its Sustainability 
Strategy, six monthly to the Board. The sustainability
programme is refreshed annually and outlines 
key initiatives to address Transpower’s key 
sustainability risks, challenges and opportunities.
1.3  Board skills and competence
The Board ensures appropriate skills and capability 
are available through a regular assessment of 
each director’s skills and competencies in core 
governance areas, including climate change. This 
is published in Transpower’s Integrated Report. 
Education is provided to boost members’ relevant 
skills and competencies where required, delivered 
by subject matter experts both internally 
and externally. 
Climate change is an area of focus for 
Transpower’s induction and ongoing education 
for its directors. Some of Transpower’s directors 
have completed formal climate- and sustainability-
related professional development and courses, 
such as the Harvard Kennedy School, Climate 
Change and Energy, Policy Making for the Long-
Term and New Zealand Institute of Directors 
– Addressing the Climate Urgency. One director 
is a member of Chapter Zero. One director has 
been a member of the Interim Climate Change 
Commission, and another is the Chair of the 
External Reporting Board and a Board member 
of Toitū Tahua: Centre for Sustainable Finance. 
Climate-related risks and opportunities are 
regularly discussed at Transpower’s Board 
meetings, which means directors are continually 
building additional knowledge and expertise in 
this area.
1.4  The role of management
The Chief Executive has overall responsibility 
for the management of Transpower. Day-to-
day management is delegated to executive 
general managers, who together make up the 
Executive Leadership Team (ELT). Executive GMs 
are responsible for assessing and managing 
risks in their respective divisions. Managers at 
each level are responsible for evaluating the risk 
environment and putting controls in place to 
prevent these risks from occurring or, once they 
have eventuated, to mitigate their impact.
The ELT is responsible for directing and providing 
assurance over Transpower’s Enterprise Risk 
Management Framework, including climate-
related risks and opportunities, with the Chief 
Financial Officer having overall responsibility 
for the framework. On a quarterly basis, the ELT 
reviews all strategic, external and key operational 
risks. The impact of a changing climate is 
reflected in all three of these risk categories, 
particularly external. The ELT reviews and updates 
key risks before these are reported to the Audit 
and Risk Committee.
The climate-related disclosure process is 
undertaken by a cross-business management 
group including members of the strategy, 
risk and assurance, sustainability, and asset 
management, finance and treasury functions. 
This group coordinates the annual update of the 
climate statement and monitors climate-related 
risks and opportunities including those that are 
new and emerging as well as changes to the 
materiality of existing ones. 
Transpower’s key risks and related strategic 
priorities are published annually in the 
Integrated Report.

2.2  Scenario analysis 
Transpower has developed, and uses, three 
climate change scenarios to help identify its 
climate-related risks and opportunities, and to 
better understand the resilience of its assets 
to climate change. 
Scenarios represent a plausible, dynamic and 
challenging range of possible futures, and allow 
key uncertainties and assumptions to be explored. 
They are not probabilistic predictions, nor snapshot 
descriptions of an end point in time. Scenarios 
support Transpower’s decision-making and 
enable Transpower to understand the resilience 
of its business model, strategies and plans. 
Transpower’s climate change scenarios are based 
on degrees of temperature rise due to global 
warming out to 2100 and consider a wide range of 
information to represent possible global, national 
and industry-specific developments. The chart 
also illustrates relative sea level rise projections in 
Aotearoa New Zealand under Transpower’s climate 
scenarios. The shading represents confidence 
intervals of the projection. Importantly, a noticeable 
divergence in scenarios is not expected until 2050, 
which is a broad proxy for other climate-related 
impacts. They are split into three-time horizons:
•	 short term (2025–2040)
•	 medium term (2040–2060)
•	 long term (2080–2100).

2.3.1  Transpower invests in the transition 
To support the country’s commitment to net-zero
emissions by 2050, the Government has an 
interim target of 50 per cent renewable energy 
by 2035. Electrification will play a key role in 
achieving both objectives, particularly in the 
electrification of two of the country’s most 
carbon-intensive sectors transport, and process 
heat. Based on current modelling, powering this 
change will mean increasing installed generation 
from about 9 GW today to approximately 22 GW 
by 2050, to meet electricity demand under the 
WiTMH Accelerated Electrification scenario. 
Transpower needs to build and enhance the 
transmission grid to ensure it can continue to 
deliver electricity from where it is generated to 
where it is needed, enable the rapid connection 
of new renewable energy sources, increase 
the capacity of the grid to support these 
connections and increasing demand and finally, 
continue to operate a stable power system that 
seamlessly integrates more highly distributed 
and intermittent energy sources. 
The investment required to maintain the existing 
grid and existing service levels for customers must 
be approved by the Commerce Commission, 
which occurs through a submission process for 
funding of five-year regulatory control periods 
following customer consultation and independent 
verification. This includes a modest amount for grid 
enhancement and development.
Separate approval is required for major capital 
projects. These costs are recovered from 
customers (electricity distributors, generators 
and certain load customers) through the 
transmission pricing methodology determined 
by the Electricity Authority. Specific connections 
for customer projects are funded under separate 
bilateral contracts.
Transpower’s Net Zero Grid Pathways programme 
is a multi-year programme of work through 
which it will investigate, plan, consult on and 
seek Commerce Commission approval for the 
required major capital projects to deliver these 
requirements. This suite of documents sets out 
the projects that, if delivered, would double the 
regulated asset base over the next 10 years. The 
programme is driven by key tactical decisions 
informed by broader long-term planning, including 
the Transmission Planning Report and Asset 
Management Plan. 
In May 2022, Transpower launched its Green 
Financing Framework, a step that ensures its 
funding strategy is aligned with its sustainability 
objectives and supports its ability to source 
the finance required to enable the investment 
needed. The Green Financing Framework 
covers both existing and future issuances of 
Transpower’s debt instruments – a debt book of 
approximately $3.2 billion as of 30 June 2024. 
2.3.2  Transpower continues to build resilience 
into its planning 
Climate-related risks are managed as part 
of Transpower’s overall asset management 
approach. An asset-risk review process identifies 
and collects information on all major hazards 
including those related to climate change. This 
enables informed decisions about asset health
and network risk, so that Transpower can 
maintain a safe and reliable network and realise 
improvements in resilience to natural hazards 
and climate change.
Risk reduction for climate-related risks regularly
occurs through upgrades and asset replacement.
However, Transpower needs to proactively invest 
in risk reduction and readiness where those 
upgrades or replacements are insufficient to 
manage the risk. Transpower’s 2025-2030 workplan
contains a proactive resilience programme which 
includes risk reduction and readiness initiatives 
for climate-related risks. Transpower is also 
developing a climate adaptation plan, which 
will build on recent work, and will identify and 
document the next phase of improvements 
relating to climate change adaptation.

Risk management
Climate-related risks have long been 
considered as part of Transpower’s 
overall risk management and it 
continues to evolve and mature 
its processes. 
3.1  Identification and assessment 
Transpower identifies and assesses climate-
related risks continually through a range of 
tools and techniques as part of its regular risk 
management process. 
Transpower conducts a comprehensive climate risk 
assessment with a range of internal stakeholders 
on an annual basis. These assessments are 
facilitated in accordance with the approach set 
out by the IPCC. All identified risks are assessed 
in detail by relevant subject matter experts and 
business owners of the risk. Where feasible and 
practical, risk is quantified in dollar terms. 
Quantification of physical risks is undertaken 
using the hazard, exposure, vulnerability, 
impact (HEVI) methodology. Quantification of 
transition risk at present is challenging due to 
a lack of available data, or a significant degree 
of uncertainty surrounding the data. As an 
alternative, metrics that relate to transition risks 
and opportunities are identified. 
As Transpower matures its understanding of 
climate-related risks and opportunities and 
acquires better information, the level of financial 
quantification provided will increase. 
3.2  Prioritisation and management of 
climate-related risks and opportunities
Climate-related risks are viewed as external 
threats to existing risks. They are prioritised in 
the same manner as all other external threats 
and managed in a similar fashion to all other 
risks at Transpower. 
Risks are assessed against the enterprise-
wide, corporate risk management matrix, 
which is derived from the Board’s Risk Appetite 
Statement, and includes environmental, social 
responsibility and good governance as key 
exposure categories.
Transpower’s risk and assurance function 
oversees an annual internal audit programme 
to provide assurance to management and the 
Board. The assurance function also includes 
undertaking self-assessments on critical controls 
for risk management.
Climate-related opportunities are prioritised in 
line with all other business opportunities as part 
of the strategy setting and review process.

4.1  Greenhouse gases 
4.1.1  Overview
As outlined in the most recent IPCC report 
(4 April 2022), to achieve the 1.5˚C of global 
warming by 2050 target, almost all electricity 
would need to be from zero- or low-carbon 
sources and more activities would need to run 
on electricity. 
Modelling in 2020 predicts electricity demand 
will grow from 42 TWh (terawatt hours) to 
70 TWh by 2050, primarily from electrifying 
transport and process heat. Future electricity 
demand may be higher if currently hard-to-
electrify sectors such as aviation are included. 
Transpower needs to replenish and replace 
our assets as they approach end of life and will 
need to invest significantly in new and upgraded 
transmission infrastructure to ensure targets are 
met. This investment will result in an increase in 
its carbon footprint.
In addition, as the grid enables the flow of 
electricity from where it is generated to where it 
is used, Transpower bears losses on behalf of the 
sector. Scope 2 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions 
associated with transmission losses are linked to 
the electricity required to compensate for them 
and are calculated according to the relative 
carbon intensity of the electricity generation 
mix, something over which Transpower has 
no control. 
Furthermore, the process of electrification may 
result in a corresponding increase in transmission 
losses borne by Transpower, even with more 
renewable generation coming onto the power 
system. This is largely a function of where the 
generation resource and plant is located, neither 
of which Transpower can control.
To illustrate the annual variability of these non-
controllable emissions, in FY2023 Transpower 
reported a 34 per cent decrease in emissions 
from transmission losses from FY2022, largely 
due to the increased volume of hydro electricity 
generation in the electricity mix over FY2023 
due to relatively high rainfall in catchment areas. 
In FY2024 Transpower reported a further 3 per 
cent decrease, reflecting a relatively similar 
carbon intensity in the generation mix to the 
previous year.
Transpower’s emissions reduction work 
programme and associated targets do not rely 
on offsets, being primarily driven by emissions 
reduction priorities. 
Enabling the move towards an increasingly 
renewable electricity system for Aotearoa 
New Zealand is the biggest contribution 
Transpower can make to reducing our 
emissions. One challenge Transpower faces 
is that, as it enables the electrification of the 
economy by building new connection points 
and upgrading the national grid, its own carbon 
footprint is set to increase substantially. This 
is due to a likely rise in transmission losses – at 
least in the immediate term – as well as an 
increase in embodied carbon as part of the 
physical construction and upgrade of network 
infrastructure. It is important to note that any 
increase of Transpower’s own carbon footprint 
will ultimately be offset by the net benefit 
of electrification to the country. Enabling 
electrification is the best way to reduce 
Aotearoa New Zealand’s overall emissions.
While Transpower’s own overall emissions 
will rise as it builds the infrastructure required 
to enable electrification, and consequently 
does not contribute to limiting global warming 
to 1.5˚C, there can be no transition without 
electricity transmission. Transpower’s increasing 
emissions are an essential byproduct of Aotearoa 
New Zealand’s electrification and are required for 
the country to meet its net-zero by 2050 target. 
Transpower has engaged with the Climate 
Leaders Coalition on this challenge and has 
received an exemption from an overall emissions 
reduction target under the Climate Leaders 
Coalition Statement of Ambition.

Grid Performance 1 and 2 (GP1 and GP2) are

These, alongside other metrics, are monitored

sub-categories during a disclosure year.
Our grid performance metrics capture all 
causes of service outages, including non-
climate-related events such as equipment 
malfunction or human error. 
Targets for both GP1 and GP2 are to achieve 
between four and six collars for occurrence. There 
are six points of service categories. Transpower 
must achieve the collar amount in at least four out 
of six of them. Collars are the level of performance 
that results in Transpower receiving the maximum 
financial penalty for the performance measure 
in question. Meeting the target for a point of 
service means that Transpower does not exceed 
the collar threshold.

Service Measures Report 2023.

Peak demand continues to grow. Six of the 
highest peaks on record occurred in 2023. 
Peak demand has risen 2 per cent annually on 
average since 2021, with another increase of 
122 MW this winter, attributed to the growing 
electrification of transport, process heat 
and space heating. It is also attributed to the 
removal of regional coincident peak demand 
(RCPD15) charges, with analysis published by 
the Electricity Authority confirming that this is 
associated with a 157 MW increase in average 
peaks – or 2.2 per cent of national demand. 
Moderate winter conditions, above average 
hydrological inflows and market coordination 
enabled the system to cope in 2023. However, 
demand is expected to continue to grow, largely 
met by new renewables such as wind and solar. 
Firming capacity will also be needed at peak 
times, as well as non-network solutions like 
demand response. This will take time to build 
and commission and have available on the
